# What SATCOM Systems Really Need From Their Motors


Low Earth Orbit (LEO) constellations and mobile connectivity are reshaping satellite communication, placing new demands on motion systems on the ground, at sea and in space. From the gimbals that keep antennas pointed at the right satellite to the reaction wheels that control a satellite’s orientation,[motors](https://allient.com/product-category/motors/) play a key role in these systems. In this interview, Robert Mastromattei, Chief Commercial Officer & Group President at Allient Inc., discusses what SATCOM systems need from their motors, and how manufacturers can reduce risk when choosing them.


**1. SATCOM covers everything from ground stations to satellites in orbit. What are the main applications for motors?**


There are a few main areas. Traditional satellite communication relies on large ground-based dishes that track geosynchronous satellites. Because these satellites move with the Earth, the motorized dish only needs small adjustments, and that is work we have done for many years.


Over roughly the last 10 to 15 years, low orbit satellites have changed the picture. Ground-based systems now track low orbit satellites, and many satellites communicate with each other using motor-driven gimbals. Satellites also typically use reaction wheels, which are essentially motor-driven inertia wheels, to control their attitude.


Then there is mobile satellite communication on aircraft and ships. There, the platform and the satellites are both moving, which requires a different kind of tracking.


**3. What are the main challenges SATCOM equipment manufacturers face today?**


Supply chain is a major challenge, because these systems depend on precision components that manufacturers can count on. Magnets are a big part of that, as most motors used in motion systems contain them.


Space applications that see wide temperature ranges and need small, lightweight designs tend to rely on higher-strength, higher-temperature magnet materials. Manufacturers need to understand where the magnets in their systems come from, whether they can obtain them, and what that means for lead time and cost.


**2. LEO constellations have changed the scale of SATCOM. What does that mean for motor demand?**


Where there were once hundreds of satellites performing communication tasks, there are now thousands. Because low orbit satellites are not geosynchronous, many more of them are needed, and because they have a shorter service life, they also need to be replenished on an ongoing basis.


Those satellites rely on motion to stay in the right orientation and, in many cases, to communicate with other satellites and the ground, while ground systems rely on motion to track them. The number of motors and motion systems has gone up significantly with low orbit satellites.


**4. How does the operating environment change what is required from the motor?**


The underlying physics of the motor does not change much between environments. The bigger differences come from selecting materials and components that can cope with each one.


At sea, salt spray is a factor, and protecting against it can dictate much of the design. On land, temperatures vary depending on location, and wind plays a part. If a dish is caught in a windstorm, the forces on it can be huge, and the motor and mechanical system still need to hold it in position.


In space there is no wind, but there are wide temperature variations, and UV and radiation that some materials cannot handle.


**5. Ground systems range from tracking pedestals to backpack-mounted terminals. What motor technologies are used in these systems?**


Ground-based systems need to track what is happening in the sky. We have traditionally done that with direct drive torque motors, such as[frameless motors](https://allient.com/product-category/motors/frameless-motors/) , integrated into the tracking pedestal. In other cases, we supply motor assemblies that drive a customer’s own gimbal.


A backpack terminal communicating with low orbit satellites needs to adjust while the user and the satellites are moving, then pick up the next satellite. For the gimbals in these terminals, small, lightweight motors, including[axial flux motors](https://allient.com/product-category/motors/frameless-motors/axial-flux-motors/) , can be well suited.


Ground systems generally do not face the same temperature cycling or efficiency requirements as space systems. Motor attributes that address those challenges are nice to have on the ground, but necessary in space.


**6. Reaction wheels keep LEO satellites in the right orientation. What does a reaction wheel motor need to deliver?**


The motor needs to run smoothly, because any vibration can be felt across the whole satellite. It also needs to be lightweight, use the correct materials for space and handle wide temperature variations.


These are not attributes that normal motors typically have, so unless a motor has been designed for space, it will usually need significant customization. Allient has motors that are designed with space applications in mind. They are lightweight, high performance and smooth running, with materials selected for space. These include the[TGR Series](https://allient.com/product/tgr-series-brushless-motors/) , a product line designed specifically for satellite reaction wheel assemblies.


**7. Allient supplies motors for both ground and space applications. What makes a motion solution stand out in SATCOM?**


Motor performance gets you in the door. Output for size has to be competitive, and no one wants to put a motor that is twice as heavy into a space application. What really stands out is experience in the application, and the lessons learned that can be applied to each customer’s project.


If you select a motor online, you may have no way of knowing whether the materials will last in space, whether it will perform or whether it will run too hot. The experience we bring to the table can help SATCOM manufacturers make the right decisions.


Allient also has a broad range of technologies and products. For many environments and applications, we have a product to suit, and when you move up to space, we have another product line for that.


**8. What will matter most to SATCOM engineers when choosing a motor supplier in the years ahead?**


At the end of the day, engineers are risk averse. When they talk to a supplier, they are assessing whether that supplier can help them mitigate the risk of a part not working, and that depends on whether the engineers on the other side truly understand the problem.


That is the difference between knowing something and understanding it. Information is easy to find and easy to share, but real understanding takes experience, and that is likely to matter even more over the next decade.
